item.title: Sparse-Blossom Decoding in o(1) Time
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Parallel sparse blossom decodes an O(d)-round syndrome extraction window on a distance-d rotated surface code in average parallel runtime bounded by exp⁡[O((log⁡log⁡d)2)], yielding o(1) average parallel runtime per round.

Grade 0.399 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Ryo Mikami, Hayata Yamasaki

Figure

Event counts per shot per syndrome extraction round plotted against code distance d∈{9,13,…,49}, demonstrating that parallel sparse-blossom runtime per round decreases with increasing d at low physical error rates.

Asks

Can minimum-weight perfect matching decoding via sparse blossom be parallelized with an exact correctness guarantee and a runtime per round that scales as o(1)?

Before

Decoding time per round scaled as O(d2.34) in sequential sparse blossom, requiring O(d3.34) total latency for a d-round window (Higgott and Gidney 2023).

But

Circuit-level local stochastic error model below a finite threshold pth, with finite-size numerical comparisons assuming negligible parallelization overhead.

Tools

parallel sparse blossom · hierarchical error clustering · minimum-weight embedded matching · rotated surface code simulation

Abstract

Matching-based decoding is widely used in quantum error correction, and accelerating it is key to enabling fast and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding provides rigorous guarantees for error suppression, while sparse blossom enables its practical implementation at modest problem sizes. However, the runtime of existing sparse-blossom implementations unavoidably increases with problem size, motivating a rigorous parallelization framework that guarantees correctness and a runtime shorter than the syndrome-extraction timescale. Here, we present such a framework and prove that the resulting parallel sparse-blossom algorithm produces the same correction as the original, non-parallel sparse blossom. For the rotated surface code with code distance d and physical error rates below a finite threshold, we prove that the average parallel runtime of decoding for O(d) rounds of syndrome extraction is upper bounded by a quasi-polylogarithmic function of d. For a d-round decoding window, this implies that the average parallel runtime per round is o(1). We also perform numerical simulation to identify conditions under which the parallel runtime per round decreases with increasing code distance. These results suggest that increasing code distance need not lead to longer parallel decoding times, providing a foundation for scalable parallel matching-based decoding.

item.title: A Simple Quantum Linear-System Solver via Dissipation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Purely dissipative Lindbladian solves Ax=b via residual-reset jumps with trace-distance mixing time Θ(κ2log⁡(1/ε)) and digital quantum query complexity O(κ2log⁡(1/ε)log⁡(κ/ε)log⁡log⁡(κ/ε)).

Grade 0.386 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations” · Zhong-Xia Shang

Figure

Schematic of population flow in the dissipative solver showing jump-induced reset to state |r⟩ and decay towards the target stationary state.

Asks

Is it possible to solve linear systems from dissipation?

Before

was O(κlog⁡(1/ε)) query complexity in coherent algorithms (Costa et al. 2022, Chakraborty et al. 2023)

But

Requires 0<ε<1/4, κ≥1, and unitary access to block encoding UA and state preparation Ub.

Tools

residual kernel encoding · purely dissipative Lindbladian · collective block encoding · Lindbladian simulation

Abstract

Dissipation has been recently demonstrated as a powerful primitive for designing quantum algorithms. We apply this viewpoint directly to linear-system solving, Ax=b. We construct a simple purely dissipative Lindbladian whose unique fixed point encodes the linear-system solution. We prove dimension-independent trace-distance mixing in Θ(κ²log(1/eps)) time. We then show how to run this Lindbladian on digital quantum computers via collective block encoding and Lindbladian simulation, resulting in an O (κ²log(1/eps) (log(κ/eps))/(loglog(κ/eps))) query complexity for both U_A, the block encoding of A, and U_b, the |b⟩ state preparation unitary.

item.title: Benchmarking the computational power of quantum computers
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Defines QUOPS to benchmark quantum capability by circuit size and execution rate. Translating utility challenge problems (factoring RSA-2048, FeMoco) shows computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude over current physical processors (Quantinuum Helios-1 Q=1504, H2-1 Q=1320).

Grade 0.381 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum supremacy using a programmable superconducting processor” · Timothy Proctor, Oliver Hart, Oliver Widzowski Maupin, Matthew Girling, Daniel Hothem, Daniel Mills, Jordan Hines, Karl Mayer, Jacob S. Nelson, Tyler LeBlond, Zohim Chandani, Diego Forlivesi, Piper C. Wysocki, Boldizsár Poór, Joan M. Dreiling, Annie Park, Adam P. Reed, Brian Estey, Cameron Foltz, Akhil Isanaka, M. S. Allman, Michael Mills, Maxwell D. Urmey, Peter E. Siegfried, Audrey Faricy, Jin-Sung Kim, Cristina Cîrstoiu, Andrew D. Baczewski, Charles H. Baldwin, Robin Blume-Kohout

Figure

Plots QUOPS capability regions (circuit size vs width), historical capability score scaling vs time with exponential trend lines showing 1.4-year (Quantinuum) and 2.1-year (IBM) doubling times, and QUOPS execution rate vs score for physical, logical, and projected architectures against utility milestones.

Asks

How can quantum computational power be directly benchmarked and compared across disparate physical and logical architectures relative to utility-scale challenge problems?

Before

Quantum volume and physical gate error rates; quantum volume scaling requires exponential classical verification and does not map directly to fault-tolerant utility resource requirements.

But

Historical score inferences rely on global depolarizing noise, two-qubit gates as the sole error source, and simplified compilation models accurate to within roughly a factor of two.

Tools

QUOPS benchmark suite · Mirror circuit fidelity estimation · Steane llbracket7,1,3rrbracket logical processor · Quantinuum Helios-1 ion-trap processor · IBM ibm_boston and Google Willow superconducting processors

Abstract

Quantum computing hardware is advancing rapidly toward utility-scale machines that will enable scientific breakthroughs. Many teams are pursuing distinct and difficult-to-compare routes to this goal, using different qubit technologies and logical architectures. Tracking progress toward quantum utility therefore requires rigorous benchmarks that measure computational capability relative to utility-scale challenge problems and enable fair comparison across disparate platforms. Here we demonstrate direct, cross-platform measurement of quantum computational capability using a new benchmark that quantifies the size of the largest computationally relevant quantum circuits that a machine can execute successfully and the speed at which it can execute them. We apply this quantum universal operation performance system (QUOPS) experimentally to leading processors from Quantinuum, Google, and IBM, computing directly on physical qubits. Translating state-of-the-art resource requirements for recognized challenge problems that represent useful quantum computation into effective QUOPS circuit sizes shows that computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude, motivating fault-tolerant approaches. We use the same benchmark to assess the performance of a simple fault-tolerant logical-qubit processor implemented on up to eight [[7,1,3]]-encoded logical qubits using Quantinuum Helios-1, and project the growth of capability across successive generations of fault-tolerant quantum computers to show how QUOPS can track progress toward quantum scientific utility.
